Then the man in the pool called for tea, and I saw an Indian monk holding half a skull, as if a melon had been cut open. Looking at it, with the brains dripping, I felt great loathing. The monk then scooped some out with his finger and showed it to me, saying: ‘Is this impure?’ and at once put it in his mouth and ate it. Thus he took and ate, and it was sweet as syrup. When the brains were all eaten, only bloody water remained. The man in the pool said: ‘You may give it to him.’ The monk then handed it to me, and I took it and drank; its taste was like sweet dew. Drinking it down, it penetrated the pores of my body, flowing out in every direction. When I had drunk, the Indian monk rubbed my back and gave a great slap with his palm, and I awoke. Then my whole body streamed with sweat like water, and my five viscera were clear. From then on body and mind were as if washed, light and quick beyond compare. Dreams such as these were mostly auspicious omens. In short, they were all exchanges
zuò
. I have once heard the Buddha’s words, ‘one often has such good dreams’ — truly so.
(Master Miaofeng seen a fifth time)
[One often has such good dreams] The Buddha said: “
The Buddhas’ bodies are golden-hued, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits. Hearing the Dharma and expounding it for others, one often has such good dreams.” (Lotus Sutra)
Fuzheng’s note: in my attendance I often saw the Patriarch’s calligraphy; both his regular and his running script were excellent, all founded on the standards of the two Wangs
(Wang Xizhi and Wang Xianzhi)
, entering and departing with flexibility and change. When he pricked his blood to write the Avatamsaka, he did not stop his brush nor refuse his guests
(did not turn away visitors)

, and with every stroke he wrote he recited the Buddha’s name once; even when talking with men of high attainment he still did not cease writing. Copying against the original and checking it, there was not a single error or omission. Without great Chan concentration and great spiritual power, how could one be utterly free of error or omission?

To speak truly of this one great dream-samādhi: in the first dream he saw the Great Master Qingliang in person, in the Vajra Grotto, leaning on the couch and giving him a prediction, and at once the realm appeared before him and body and mind were without obstruction. This accords with the earlier record of his never forgetting Qingliang and never forgetting the karmic bond with Master Miao.

In the second dream he came to the Tuṣita heaven and the pavilion of Maitreya; he saw with his own eyes the adorned jewel seat, and Maitreya Buddha commanded a monk to give him the sutra. He ascended the seat and, face to face, heard the teaching of defilement and purity, clear in his ears, and at once the distinction between consciousness and wisdom was clear to his mind and eye.

In the third dream he went in person to the bath prepared by Mañjuśrī on the summit of the North Peak. His disgust at the woman and her floating forth as a man was simply the Patriarch’s own manifestation of a boy’s untouched body. Single-minded and undistracted, originally pure, without the least entanglement or defilement, he was able to enter the ocean of fragrant water and shed his skin and change his bones. Yet again the dream showed forth fair and foul, pure and impure; fright and loathing, love and attachment, and all manner of marks, transformed and made strange to the uttermost, so that the five colors had no master.

In the end it is like Fotudeng, who at the water’s edge broke open his chest and washed his stomach and intestines clean, so that his body was transparent as crystal. In the end it is like Huangbo and Linji, each blow leaving its mark, each slap its blood. In the end it is like Xuanni
(Confucius)

seeing King Wen and the Duke of Zhou in person. Long and short, black and white, eyes open and eyes shut — none of it is other than true dream. With clarity within him and his will and spirit like a god’s, the real is the dream real, and the dream is the real dream; therefore it is said that the utmost man has no dreams.
[Fotudeng]

The Lives of Eminent Monks records: “When Dao’an first came to Ye, he entered the Zhong Temple and met Fotudeng; at the first sight of An, Cheng recognized his worth, and they talked together all day.”

Nevertheless, had he not cast aside body and life and dwelt deep in the heaps of ice and snow, buried alive for six years and all but dead many times over, how could he have come to life out of death, lifted his head out of the great dream, wrapped heaven and enclosed earth, illumined the past and shone upon the present, and become a man beyond measure? Had he not, at the place on the ridge of Dayu where the robe and bowl were seized
(Huiming seizing the Sixth Patriarch’s robe and bowl; see
“A Detailed Explanation of the Sixth Patriarch’s Platform Sutra”

, died and been born again, passing through three turns and nine revolutions and renewing two temples, how could he today sit upright in his flesh body, manifest at Caoxi, seal in the north at Qingliang, and in the south keep company with Patriarch Lu
(the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, called Patriarch Lu because his family name was Lu)
Hanshan’s Dharma-word says: ‘From the tip of a single hair, a Buddha-realm of jewels wells forth.’
(the Patriarch said: “Suddenly I saw at the tip of a single hair the appearance of the jewel king’s realm.” (From the Dream-Roaming Collection
‘Memorial on Rebuilding the Halls of the Patriarch’s Court at Caoxi’))
On the day when he took up his brush and spread out his paper
chǔ
, a term for paper)

to set down his own chronicle, he was no more than one austere old man within the four seas, one who had taken refuge in the venerable elders. Monks of Chan in every quarter, seeing the chronicle of the three dreams in his lifetime, would surely laugh and call it raving. Hearing the account of the three dreams after his passing, they would go so far as to denounce it as a demon-realm. Only the Patriarch himself could believe it; in all the world and in after ages there was certainly not one man who could believe it. But now
(the Patriarch has already attained the indestructible vajra body)

we know that Maitreya’s giving of the sutra fully confirms that the future kalpa is as the kalpa without beginning, and that Mañjuśrī’s preparing of the bath was to bathe this skin-and-flesh body into a solid body. When Fuzheng’s commentary reaches this point, he is dazed as in a dream, entering Caoxi. In the inexpressible, inexpressible, inconceivable, he joins his palms once more and says: ‘Rare indeed, World-Honored One.’
Wanli, seventh year
CE),
jǐmǎo ●
I was thirty-four. In the autumn of that year the Great Cishou Temple in the capital was completed. At first the Holy Mother, to make offering for the late Emperor and to protect the imperial person
(to sacrifice to the late Emperor and to bless the present sovereign)
, wished to build the Tayuan Temple and the precious relic stupa at Mount Wutai. She instructed the ministers,
who considered
Mount Wutai too far from the capital
(distant)

, and so a lucky site near the capital was divined, and the Great Cishou Temple was built. When the work was done, it was reported back. The Holy Mother, thinking the vow to Mount Wutai unfulfilled, instructed the Emperor, who again sent eunuch officials with three thousand workmen and craftsmen to the mountain to build. At that time the court had but lately begun to do Buddhist works, and eunuch officials had but lately been sent outside; it was feared they could not finish the task, and that it would injure the Dharma-gate. At that time I did all I could to mediate and protect, and to the end nothing went amiss.
(The Holy Mother seen a second time. The late Emperor is Longqing
(Muzong of the Ming)
, seen once. The Emperor is Wanli
(Shenzong of the Ming)
, seen once.)
